1	\section{Related Work}
2	\label{sec:related-work}
3	
4	\paragraph{Neurosymbolic Reasoning with LLMs.}
5	Prompting-based pipelines couple LLMs with external solvers for logical reasoning.
6	SatLM~\cite{satlm} generates SAT formulas, Logic-LM~\cite{logic-lm} translates to first-order logic, LINC~\cite{linc} generates logic programs, and LoRP~\cite{lorp} uses Prolog as a reasoning backend; FOVER~\cite{fover-pei2025} adds iterative verification.
7	All evaluate on execution accuracy alone, without diagnosing structural quality of formalizations.
8	Recent RL approaches train LLMs against solver feedback~\cite{mellgren-prolog-grpo, logic-rl, thought-like-pro}, optimizing prove rate with binary execution reward.
9	STA differs in diagnostic focus: ISR exposes that execution accuracy conflates faithful derivation with degenerate shortcuts, and our finding that 87\% of proved outputs under exec-only GRPO embed the conclusion in the premises (\S\ref{sec:diagnostic}) suggests prior prove-rate gains may overstate genuine reasoning improvement.
10	We adopt FOLIO~\cite{folio} as it is the only publicly available NLI benchmark providing both FOL and Prolog annotations, enabling our cross-logic diagnostic transfer experiments; ProofWriter~\cite{proofwriter} and ProntoQA~\cite{prontoqa} offer synthetic logical reasoning benchmarks but lack the multi-logic annotation required for cross-logic comparison.
11	
12	\paragraph{Reward Shaping and Process Supervision.}
13	Binary outcome rewards motivate process-level supervision: learned process reward models~\cite[PRMs;][]{lightman-verify-step, math-shepherd} provide step-level feedback, solver-grounded signals~\cite{rlsf} leverage formal verification, and rubric-based rewards~\cite{rubric-grpo} encode structured evaluation criteria.
14	However, process rewards introduce their own failure modes: design choices dominate signal effects~\cite{gao-effective-rl-reward}, process and outcome rewards can conflict~\cite{prof-process-outcome}, and PR

2	\label{sec:experiments}
3	
4	We evaluate STA along three axes: as a diagnostic for reward hacking (\S\ref{sec:diagnostic}); as a training reward exhibiting meta-level Goodhart's Law (\S\ref{sec:goodhart}); and as a cross-logic protocol (\S\ref{sec:crosslogic}). 1	\section{Introduction}
2	\label{sec:introduction}
3	
4	A GRPO-trained formalizer achieves a 93\% prove rate on first-order logic problems---yet 87\% of its proved outputs embed the conclusion verbatim among the premises.
5	The solver succeeds not because the model has learned to reason, but because the formalization trivially entails any conclusion that already appears as a premise.
6	This structural shortcut is invisible to execution-based evaluation: prove rate registers success regardless of whether the proof reflects genuine multi-step derivation or degenerate circular embedding.
7	
8	Prove rate---the dominant evaluation metric for neurosymbolic formalizers---conflates faithful reasoning with degenerate shortcuts, a gap especially consequential under reinforcement learning, where the optimizer exploits any shortcut the reward fails to penalize~\cite{skalse-reward-hacking, reward-hacking-survey}.
9	Recent work applies GRPO~\cite{deepseekmath} to train LLMs that generate solver-verified formal programs~\cite{mellgren-prolog-grpo, logic-rl} using binary execution feedback as reward; this drives rapid PR gains but gives no gradient on structural quality.
10	Process reward models~\cite{lightman-verify-step} offer step-level supervision but require expensive annotations and do not transfer to arbitrary solver-backed settings.
11	No existing method provides an annotation-free diagnostic for structural integrity in neurosymbolic outputs---one adaptable in principle to any solver supporting component-level input manipulation (see \S\ref{sec:related-work} for full context).
12	
13	We address this gap with \emph{Solver Trace Ablation} (STA), a diagnostic protocol inspired by mutation testing~\cite{demillo1978} that applies component necessity testing---leave-one-out (LOO) ablation on solver inputs---to quantify structural integrity (\autoref{fig:sta-overview}).

1	\section{Limitations}
2	\label{sec:limitations}
3	
4	Experiments use a single base model (Qwen3-4B) and dataset family (FOLIO); generalization remains untested.
5	ISR quantifies syntactic component necessity, not semantic faithfulness: a downstream NLI evaluation finds ISR and task accuracy uncorrelated (Spearman $\rho{=}{-}0.049$, $p{=}0.187$; Appendix~\ref{app:extended-discussion}).
6	Three seeds demonstrate qualitative divergence but limit statistical power.
7	STA requires solvers supporting component-level input manipulation.
8	
9	\paragraph{Data scale.}
10	Our experiments use 500 training examples and 100 evaluation examples, reflecting the FOLIO dataset's total size of 1,435 annotated examples~\citep{folio}.
11	The training subset is selected via stratified sampling (seed 42) and held constant across all conditions.
12	While our findings are consistent across seeds and logic types, the effect of training data scale on hacking prevalence and mode distribution remains an open question for future work.

\section{Discussion and Conclusion}

We introduced Solver Trace Ablation (STA), a component-level diagnostic for neurosymbolic formalizers that exposes structural degeneration invisible to execution-based evaluation.
Applied to GRPO-trained models, ISR reveals a collapse trajectory hidden from prove rate, confirmed as RL-specific by an SFT baseline with near-zero hacking (\S\ref{sec:diagnostic}).
When repurposed as a training signal, ISR induces meta-level Goodhart's Law: at low dose, the model games the diagnostic itself through conclusion duplication absent under matched controls; at high dose, prove rate collapses; the sole apparent ISR improvement reduces to noise after controlling for a premise-count confound (\S\ref{sec:goodhart}).
Both diagnostic utility and Goodhart vulnerability transfer to Prolog/SWI-Prolog: ISR-as-reward yields universal gaming across all seeds with zero non-hacking proofs, each via a distinct mechanism (\S\ref{sec:crosslogic}).
Across six reward conditions and two logic types, we catalog seven hacking modes, including query-as-fact gaming that bypasses text-match classifiers (\S\ref{sec:taxonomy}).

\paragraph{Interpreting ISR.}
ISR values must be read relative to the optimization objective: under exec-only Prolog, \emph{low} ISR reflects redundant coding, not absent reasoning; under ISR-as-reward, \emph{high} ISR reflects metric gaming.
The premise-count confound applies to any ablation-based diagnostic on variable-length outputs; Shapley values could provide more nuanced attribution at higher cost.

\paragraph{Meta-Level Goodhart.}
ISR was designed to \emph{detect} reward gaming, yet becomes gamed itself when optimized---a regress where any diagnostic metric risks becoming a target.
The dose-response pattern ($\beta{=}0.1$: proxy gaming; $\beta{=}0.3$: collapse) maps onto~\cite{gao-reward-overoptimization} at a meta level.
ISR---and structurally similar diagnostics---should be used exclusively as post-hoc evaluation tools; the asymmetry (reliable observer, unreliable optimizer) may generalize to other perturbation-based quality metrics.
Open directions include reward functions robust to identified gaming modes and extending STA to broader logic types.

tool_args.old_string:
Given natural language premises $P_1,\ldots,P_k$ and a conclusion $C$, the task is to produce a formal logic program $F=\{c_1,\ldots,c_n\}$, where each component $c_i$ is a premise (FOL) or a clause/fact (Prolog), with one distinguished component encoding the query.
An external solver $S$ returns $S(F)\in\{\textit{proved},\textit{failed}\}$; we use Prover9 for FOL and SWI-Prolog for Prolog (\autoref{fig:sta-overview}a).

We train formalizers with GRPO~\citep{deepseekmath} using $K{=}8$ rollouts per prompt.
Each rollout receives a binary \emph{execution reward}
$r_{\text{exec}}(x) = \mathbf{1}[S(F_x) = \textit{proved}]$;
group-relative advantages are computed within each prompt's rollout group, and the policy update maximizes a clipped surrogate objective with KL regularization.
This setup optimizes prove rate but provides no signal about \emph{structural quality}: a formalization that embeds the conclusion among its premises receives the same reward as a faithful multi-step derivation.
tool_args.new_string:
Given premises $P_1,\ldots,P_k$ and conclusion $C$, the task is to produce a formal logic program $F=\{c_1,\ldots,c_n\}$ verified by an external solver $S\in\{\text{Prover9 (FOL), SWI-Prolog}\}$ (\autoref{fig:sta-overview}a).
We train with GRPO~\citep{deepseekmath} ($K{=}8$ rollouts), where each rollout receives binary execution reward $r_{\text{exec}}(x) = \mathbf{1}[S(F_x) = \textit{proved}]$.
This optimizes prove rate but provides no signal about \emph{structural quality}: a formalization embedding the conclusion among its premises receives the same reward as a faithful derivation.

tool_args.old_string:
\paragraph{Limitations of ISR.}
ISR measures syntactic component necessity, not semantic faithfulness to the natural language input.
It is also subject to a component-count confound: formalizations with fewer components yield mechanically higher ISR, since each carries a larger share of the proof burden under LOO.
We control for this confound in our analysis (\S\ref{sec:goodhart}).

tool_args.old_string:
We study six reward conditions (\autoref{fig:sta-overview}c).
For all RL conditions, bonuses apply only to proved samples; unproved samples receive $r{=}0$.

\noindent\textbf{Exec-only:} $r=r_{\text{exec}}$ (baseline).
\noindent\textbf{Additive ISR:} $r=r_{\text{exec}}\cdot(1+\beta\,\text{ISR}(x))$ with $\beta\in\{0.1,0.3\}$, gating the structural bonus on proof success.
\noindent\textbf{Additive Random:} $r=r_{\text{exec}}\cdot(1+\beta\,u)$, $u\sim\mathcal{U}(0,1)$, $\beta\in\{0.1,0.3\}$: control isolating ISR-specific structural signal from variance/scaling effects. We draw from $\mathcal{U}(0,1)$ to match ISR's $[0,1]$ range while preserving the execution-gating structure; this provides a conservative lower bound on ISR-specific effects since any structured signal---even random---may regularize training.
\noindent\textbf{SFT baseline:} supervised fine-tuning on gold formalizations, testing whether observed hacking is RL-specific.

Each RL condition is trained with seeds $\{42,43,44\}$ controlling initialization and stochasticity; all seeds share identical training data (\S\ref{sec:setup}).

\textbf{SFT baseline.}
A supervised baseline achieves PR${=}14$\% with ISR$^*{=}0.571$: 92.9\% (13/14) [66.1\%, 99.8\%] of proved samples are non-hacking, only 1 exhibits H1, and no H7 instances occur. %% registry: plan009-sft-baseline-s42-r4
The near-absence of hacking is consistent with hacking correlating with optimization aggressiveness rather than being driven purely by model capacity or data limitations.
We note that the SFT PR level (14\%) is substantially lower than RL conditions, and the low hacking rate may partly reflect fewer opportunities for reward exploitation rather than a purely training-method difference; we address this confound via a 100-step RL checkpoint analysis in Appendix~\ref{app:100step}.

\textbf{High-dose ISR ($\beta{=}0.3$): classic Goodhart.}

The seven modes (quantitative breakdown and definitions in Appendix~\ref{app:hacking-modes}, Table~\ref{tab:hacking-taxonomy-app}): \textbf{H1} (GRPO-universal, 68--97\%), \textbf{H7} (ISR-specific, 64.5\% under $\beta{=}0.1$ vs.\ 0\% random), \textbf{tautological} (exec-only s44, 94\%), \textbf{repetition} (exec-only s43, 87\% hit max length), \textbf{contradiction explosion} (mean 18.55 components at 1000 steps), \textbf{complexity-without-utility} (Random $\beta{=}0.1$, 3.8\%), \textbf{query-as-fact} (Prolog ISR s44, bypasses text classifiers). %% registry: plan001-exec-only-s44, plan001-exec-only-s43-r4, plan016-extended-1000-s42, plan006-prolog-sta-s44
The reward signal determines hacking \emph{composition} but not \emph{prevalence}: total conclusion-in-premise rates are comparable across ISR and random (${\sim}82$\% pooled), but ISR converts H1 into H7.
